headline: Former Barclays host Malley argues ESLR relaxation is an overdue cleanup exercise needed to restore US Treasury market functioning, not broad deregulation
reasoning: Malley argues that the post-GFC regulatory regime, while individually well-intentioned, produced rules that don't always work coherently together. He frames the ESLR relaxation as restoring the leverage ratio to its intended backstop role rather than primary constraint, particularly given that the safe assets now held by large banks are predominantly US Treasuries and Fed reserves — genuinely safe instruments unlike the structured products of the crisis era. He also highlights that the Treasury market has suffered repeated bouts of dysfunction (2019, COVID, 2023 regional bank crisis) partly because large banks were balance-sheet constrained and unable to absorb selling pressure, a problem that will worsen as US deficit issuance expands.
quote: I think what we're missing here is another dimension, which is that policymakers are very worried about some recent episodes of dysfunction in the treasury market. Now, keep in mind, the treasury market, that means, you know, US government-issued debt. That is supposed to be the deepest and most liquid market in the world. But really, over the past sort of six or seven years, it hasn't always worked like that... The largest banks were constrained. They couldn't step in and buy those treasuries, precisely because of the leverage ratio that was binding. Now, fast forward six years. The US government has issued trillions more in debt thanks to the huge deficits that we have been running and continue to run. The capacity to trade all these treasuries is even more limited now, simply because the size of the market has grown by some.
episode_title: Are post-crisis US bank regulations holding markets back?

headline: Barclays Research argues US bank deregulation (ESLR relaxation, Basel III US implementation) will boost bank profitability but capacity gains may flow to buybacks rather than organic growth
reasoning: Brad Rogoff notes that post-GFC rules reduced large US bank return on equity from ~15-16% to ~9-10%, and the current round of regulatory changes — including relaxing the enhanced supplementary leverage ratio (ESLR) and the US Basel III implementation effective January — should relieve pressure on returns. However, he is skeptical that additional balance sheet capacity will translate into organic growth, citing evidence that banks have preferred returning capital to shareholders rather than reinvesting as returns fell. He draws an analogy to capital discipline in the energy sector, where shareholders have persistently demanded payouts over reinvestment even during boom periods.
quote: Look, I think the biggest effect will be an improvement in bank profitability. And I kind of like to measure that as a return on equity. So before the crisis was pretty high, kind of around 15, 16%. But since the new rules took effect, it fell a lot, kind of in the nine to 10% range. These changes should take some of the pressure off, which will be good for bank equity holders. But I think a lot of the benefit will show up higher returns, buybacks and capital distributions rather than a meaningful increase in organic growth.
episode_title: Are post-crisis US bank regulations holding markets back?

headline: Barclays Research sees US large bank risk-reward improving as deregulation lifts returns without materially increasing risk, but notes banks compete for capital against AI-sector returns
reasoning: Rogoff argues that because the current round of regulatory changes does not materially raise bank risk — a point both speakers agree on — the risk-reward trade-off improves as returns rise from the deregulation. He acknowledges that large bank shareholders have persistently demanded capital returns rather than reinvestment, but notes the analogy to larger regional banks (which improved risk-reward after post-GFC rules and did reinvest more) may apply. He also flags that banks face stiff competition for investor capital from AI-related sectors offering high expected returns, which complicates any shift back to reinvestment.
quote: The challenge is that banks are competing for investor capital at a time when some of the highest expected returns, they're not being generated in the financial sectors. They're being generated particularly in AI related sectors... It's not whether banks necessarily become riskier, but whether a safer banking system can still provide enough capacity for a rapidly growing just overall financial market. Something we're gonna be watching very carefully and following how these rule changes ultimately affect banks.
episode_title: Are post-crisis US bank regulations holding markets back?

headline: Barclays tech analysts forecast over $1 trillion in AI capex by 2028, creating significant equity and credit market activity that banks can benefit from
reasoning: Rogoff cites Barclays' own technology research forecasting more than $1 trillion in AI capital expenditure by 2028, arguing this will generate substantial activity in equity and credit markets that large banks are well-positioned to capture. He uses this as a counterargument to the concern that banks will struggle to find attractive reinvestment opportunities, suggesting that AI-driven capital market volumes could absorb additional bank capacity without compressing margins.
quote: Barclays tech analysts expect more than 1 trillion in AI CapEx by 2028. So there's gonna be plenty of activity in equity and credit markets to drive return for banks. They can kind of piggyback all of this. Okay, sure, AI is like the main focus right now, but banks are not just total bystanders in what's happening in that sector.
episode_title: Are post-crisis US bank regulations holding markets back?

headline: Malley warns that ESLR capacity created by the rule revision could be exhausted within 18 months given current US deficit trajectory, risking further rounds of deregulation
reasoning: Malley argues that if policymakers' true motivation is market functioning rather than simply cleaning up redundant rules, the current changes may be only the first round. Given the scale of ongoing US deficit spending and Treasury issuance, the SLR capacity unlocked by revisions could be consumed in roughly 18 months, potentially forcing regulators to repeatedly choose between bank stability and market stability. He also notes that interest rate risk on safe assets (as demonstrated by Silicon Valley Bank's failure) remains a live concern even for Treasury holdings.
quote: But if I'm right about the motivation, this could be the first of several rounds of revisions, as policymakers are continually forced to choose between bank stability and market stability. And the reason goes back to all that debt we're issuing and the major deficits we're running, which is that the stability concerns may keep bubbling up as the government keeps issuing. For example, the SLR capacity has been created by the revision to the rules will be used up in like 18 months, given the deficits that we're running today.
episode_title: Are post-crisis US bank regulations holding markets back?

headline: Rogoff sees ongoing US Treasury issuance demand as structurally supportive for bank trading margins despite concern about reinvestment discipline
reasoning: Rogoff argues that the sheer volume of US Treasury and other bond issuance, driven by persistent fiscal deficits, creates sustained demand for bank intermediation in low-risk fixed income markets. He believes this structural demand will absorb additional bank balance sheet capacity unlocked by ESLR relaxation without forcing down trading margins, differentiating the Treasury market opportunity from other areas where increased competition might compress returns.
quote: Remember, we were talking about all the bond issuance that's happening. As US Treasury and other entities issue more bonds, the demand to trade and finance these low risk assets grows. And I don't really see margins in that business being put under pressure. There's so much issuance, so much demand to trade and finance that stuff that I think all this extra bank capacity will be put to good use without actually forcing their returns down.
episode_title: Are post-crisis US bank regulations holding markets back?

headline: Rajdox flags that with 17 FOMC members still speaking publicly, Warsh's communication reform may simply create noisier and less coordinated forward guidance rather than eliminating it
reasoning: Even if the chair stops providing formal guidance, regional Fed presidents continue to give speeches, media interviews, and publish their own forecasts every week. This means the market has not lost forward guidance but gained 17 uncoordinated sources of it, potentially making the signal noisier and harder to interpret. Rajdox sees this as a significant practical wrinkle that undermines the intellectual elegance of Warsh's approach, though he acknowledges a glass-half-full interpretation where genuine dispersion of views forces markets to do their own analytical work.
quote: Warsh has stopped giving all guidance, but have the other 17 FOMC members because last time I checked, there are still a bunch of regional fed presidents giving speeches every week, doing media interviews, publishing their own forecasts. If the chair goes quiet, but everyone else keeps talking, you haven't eliminated forward guidance, you've just made it noisier, less coordinated... you've gone, Brad, from one person guiding the market to 17 people confusing it.
episode_title: If the Fed goes quiet, do markets make more noise?

headline: Rajdox sees the dot plot as fundamentally broken and concedes there is a genuine case for scrapping it entirely
reasoning: Rajdox notes the dot plot has become a crutch for both the Fed and markets — the Fed feels obligated to produce it, markets feel obligated to trade it, and it is wrong more often than it is right because it depends on economic forecasts being realised. He acknowledges the surprising admission from Warsh himself that the dot plot doesn't help him conduct policy, and agrees this is a remarkable statement. He draws a distinction between fixing the dot plot versus abandoning it, but concedes the intellectual case for scrapping it is genuine.
quote: The dot plot has become a crutch for the fed and for markets. The fed feels obligated to produce it, markets feel obligated to trade it, and it is wrong more often than it's right. So look, there is a genuine case for scrapping it entirely... we agree the dot plot is broken. I think we disagree on whether the answer is to fix it or bud. I can tell you what Warsh thinks. His answer is clearly the burn it can.
episode_title: If the Fed goes quiet, do markets make more noise?

headline: Rajdox warns that Warsh's refusal to articulate any reaction function — not just forward guidance — risks complete opacity and potential flash crash when the first surprise policy move hits
reasoning: Rajdox draws a key distinction between forward guidance (here is what we will do) and a reaction function (here is how we think), arguing you can scrap the former without scrapping the latter. Warsh has effectively scrapped both, refusing at his first press conference to explain how he weighs inflation versus growth or what would trigger a hike or cut. Without a reaction function to anchor expectations, Rajdox warns that the first time Warsh surprises markets, the repricing will not be gentle — potentially a flash crash or taper tantrum equivalent — because all shock absorbers have been removed.
quote: There's a difference between dropping forward guidance and refusing to articulate your reaction function at all. Forward guidance says, here's what we will do next. A reaction function says, here's how we think. And those are very different things. You can scrap the first without scrapping the second... At his very first press conference as chair, he was asked directly, how do you weigh inflation versus growth? What would make you hike? What would make you cut? And he basically refused to answer... that's not a type of honesty that helps you price a two year bond... Without even a reaction function to anchor expectations, you could get a flash crash, a taper tantrum, whatever you want to call it. The shock absorbers have been removed.
episode_title: If the Fed goes quiet, do markets make more noise?

headline: Barclays chairman of research Ajay Rajdox broadly supports Fed Chair Warsh's scrapping of forward guidance but warns execution risk is high given current macro environment
reasoning: Rajdox argues the diagnosis behind Warsh's move is correct: forward guidance turned markets into a mirror reflecting Fed speak rather than pricing real economic risk, and the Fed's forecasting track record has been consistently poor. He notes the dot plot has been wrong more often than right, and that guidance tools originally designed for zero-lower-bound crisis conditions have persisted inappropriately into a 3.5% rate environment. However, he flags significant execution risk given simultaneous oil shock, 4.2% CPI, and extreme semiconductor volatility, warning that removing the reaction function entirely—not just forward guidance—risks a market accident. He also raises the concern that if only the chair goes quiet while 17 other FOMC members keep speaking, forward guidance becomes noisier rather than disappearing. Ultimately he concludes both sides have a point: the status quo is broken but the transition is risky.
quote: I think the diagnosis is probably very right, Brad. So look, he has put his finger on something that a lot of us in markets have felt for years. When every investor on the planet is parsing Jerome Powell's adjectives, did he say some further progress, or modest further progress, or something along those lines? You have lost the plot. Markets are not pricing risk anymore. They are pricing just Fed speak. I actually thought I was gonna be the one here who was defending worse... I agree with the diagnosis. I'm less sure about the prescription, because like you said, ripping the bandage off in one go, in the middle of an oil shock with CPI at 4.2%, with the semiconductor complex moving up and down 5% a day, that's bold. I would say that's probably too bold.
episode_title: If the Fed goes quiet, do markets make more noise?

headline: Removing forward guidance risks higher term premium, wider credit spreads, and elevated rate volatility — a real economic cost Warsh may have underweighted
reasoning: Rajdox argues that if the Fed provides no framework for pricing the future, term premiums in bonds will rise, increasing mortgage rates, corporate borrowing costs, and credit spreads. He frames this not as a theoretical concern but as a tangible economic cost imposed in the name of intellectual purity. He questions whether Warsh has fully thought through this trade-off, though he also acknowledges that artificially suppressed term premiums via guidance encouraged excessive risk-taking and leverage that could eventually lead to bubbles.
quote: Markets do need some framework for pricing the future. If the Fed tells you nothing, literally nothing about where rates are heading. What happens to the term premium in bonds? I see I can answer that one, goes up. It goes up and rate volatility costs more. And that is not free. Higher term premium means higher mortgage rates, higher corporate borrowing costs, wider credit spreads. You are, it seems theoretical Brad, but you are imposing a real cost on the economy in the name of intellectual purity. And I don't know if that is a trade off that Warsh has thought through.
episode_title: If the Fed goes quiet, do markets make more noise?
